A high-quality vacuum cleaner can make all the difference for keeping your car’s interior spotless. Unlike household vacuums, car-specific models are designed to tackle heavier debris in tight spaces. However, with so many options available, choosing the right one can be overwhelming. It’s important to consider key features that affect performance and convenience to make an informed decision.

Three of the most crucial factors to evaluate are suction power, which determines how effectively the vacuum picks up dirt; attachments and accessories, which help clean hard-to-reach areas; and the power source, which impacts portability and run time.

Understanding these features will help you find a vacuum that best suits your needs, whether you prioritize strong suction for deep cleaning, versatile tools for detail work, or the malleability of a hose. Let’s dive into these essential features to ensure you choose the right car vacuum cleaner for the job.

Suction power is the most critical factor in a car vacuum because vehicle interiors can become a nightmare with everything we drag in and out of them. Unlike home carpets, car surfaces are filled with a million little spaces, textured upholstery, and stubborn floor mats that anything you can think of clings to. A vacuum with weak suction won’t be able to extract dirt that’s ground into these surfaces, leaving your car looking only half clean. Not ideal.

Additionally, higher suction power means faster, more efficient cleaning. Instead of repeatedly going over the same spot, a strong vacuum gets the job done in fewer passes, saving you time and effort. It also helps tackle heavier things such as leaves, sand, or pebbles. If you take your car’s cleanliness seriously (or don’t want to spend forever vacuuming), a high-powered vacuum is the way to go.

Attachments and accessories are essential in a car vacuum because car interiors are full of tight spaces and tricky surfaces that a standard nozzle can’t handle. Unlike home vacuums, which deal with flat carpets and open areas, a car vacuum must navigate between seats, air vents, and cup holders, all of which require specialized tools.

For example, a crevice tool helps reach between and along door panels, while a brush attachment is perfect for loosening dust from dashboards. Wide nozzles quickly work on large areas like a trunk, and wet/dry tools handle accidents before they become permanent stains. The right attachments don’t just make cleaning easier; they ensure you’re getting every last crumb out of your ride, leaving it truly spotless.

The power source of a car vacuum determines its suction strength, mobility, and convenience. Corded (AC-powered) vacuums offer the strongest suction but require an outlet and may limit movement. Cordless (battery-powered) models provide maximum portability for quick cleanups but often have weaker suction and limited run time.

Vacuums that plug into a car’s 12-volt outlet are great for on-the-go use but generally lack the power of AC models. Choosing the right type depends on your needs, such as going corded for power, cordless for convenience, or 12-volt for in-car accessibility.

The ThisWorx portable car vacuum routinely came up as the one to avoid. Its low suction didn’t do much, leaving most of the dirt and dust behind. While it is inexpensive, you do indeed get what you pay for.

The same goes for generic no-name vacuums on Amazon. While they are more affordable, they are also unreliable and often break within months of purchase.

We focused on suction power, attachments, and ease of use for this test. Using substantially dirty floor mats as our starting point, we taped them off to determine which vacuum was the most powerful. These mats were full of dirt, dust, pebbles, and dog fur; they were pretty much littered with what you might encounter in your vehicle. This strategy helped us quickly determine which vacuums were up to the task.

Our garage in New Brunswick, New Jersey, was the ideal backdrop for this test. Not only was it still dirty from summer trips, it also allowed me to spread out the old and very used floor mats I’d be using. While this test focused on how effectively the vacuums would clean up cars, a happy surprise was that they also cleaned the garage.

For this test, we reached out to pros to see what products they prefer. After determining fan favorites, digging around forums, and connecting with detailers we’ve worked with in the past, we devised a list of items to review. (You know you’re headed in the right direction when you hear the same brand or product come up multiple times.) This is how we arrived at Chemical Guys, Adam’s, Bissell, and Shark—solid and reliable brands. Metrovac popped up in my digging as a reliable shop vac in a popular Reddit group (r/AutoDetailing). They weren’t wrong.

We didn’t look at handheld car vacuums in this test. While they’re tops for convenience, they would be a separate category to investigate, given their variety. We did keep convenience in mind when picking the units we wanted to focus on, but this test was done with serious garage owners and car enthusiasts in mind.

When we reviewed the Car+Boat from Dyson, we were immensely impressed at how well the mini-vac lived up to its brand’s legacy. With legendary suction power, the Dyson was as much a revelation for car lovers as the company’s larger vacuums were for homeowners all those years ago.

Portable, lightweight, and affordable. What more could you want in a car vac? With a 20-volt MAX Li-ion battery and extra-long crevice tool, it’s as great for the car as it is around the house.

Looking for a little more power than a portable cordless vacuum can provide? Pick up this mini-utility shop vac from Armor All. It’s far more convenient than lugging around a larger shop vac, has a washable filter, and doubles as a blower.

When choosing a car or garage vacuum, size and capacity are crucial factors that impact performance and convenience. A vacuum with anywhere from two to six gallons of capacity is usually sufficient for car detailing, providing enough volume for typical debris while remaining lightweight and portable. Smaller vacuums are easier to maneuver inside a car and can be stored conveniently in a garage or trunk.

A 10-plus-gallon shop vacuum is better for garage use or frequent heavy-duty cleaning. These larger models can handle bigger messes, including sawdust, metal shavings, and wet spots, without requiring frequent emptying. They also typically feature more powerful motors for increased suction. However, they take up more storage space and may be less portable. If you need a balance between power and maneuverability, a mid-size vacuum can provide strong suction without being too bulky.

While a regular household vacuum might seem convenient for cleaning your car or garage, it often lacks the necessary power, durability, and specialized attachments for effective cleaning in these environments. Household vacuums are designed primarily for indoor surfaces such as carpets and hardwood floors, meaning they may struggle to pick up messes commonly found in cars and garages. Their shorter hoses and bulkier designs can make it challenging to reach tight spaces.

Dedicated car vacuums and shop vacuums are better suited for these tasks, offering more powerful suction, longer hoses, and attachments specifically designed for automotive cleaning. These vacuums are built with durability, often featuring rugged designs that can withstand dust, moisture, and rough handling in a garage setting. While household vacuums may work in a pinch for light cleaning, investing in a purpose-built car or garage vacuum ensures more efficient cleaning and a longer-lasting machine.

HEPA (high-efficiency particulate air) filters are essential when purchasing a car or garage vacuum, especially if you are concerned about air quality. Standard vacuum filters may struggle to trap fine particles such as dust, pollen, pet dander, and mold spores, which can get released back into the air during cleaning.

HEPA filters, however, are designed to capture at least 99.97 percent of particles, making them highly effective at reducing allergens and airborne contaminants. This is particularly beneficial if you suffer from allergies.

For car and garage cleaning, a HEPA or high-efficiency filtration system can also help keep your vehicle’s interior and your garage workspace cleaner by preventing fine dust from resettling. While HEPA-filtered vacuums may be slightly more expensive, they offer significant benefits for maintaining a healthier environment.

#4667. Yamaha unveils new NMAX E, bringing electric power to its popular motorbike lineup

Yamaha is expanding its electric two-wheeler lineup with a much more capable machine, unveiling the new NMAX E as an electric version of its popular NMAX sport scooter.

The 2027 Yamaha NMAX E is being positioned as a 125cc-equivalent electric scooter, putting it firmly above the low-speed urban electric scooters that have made up much of Yamaha’s electric lineup thus far.

At its heart is Yamaha’s new compact eAxle drive unit, which sends power to the rear wheel through a belt drive. The electric motor produces 6.7 kW (9 hp) of nominal power and peaks at 7.5 kW (10 hp), along with 33.3 Nm (24.6 lb-ft) of torque.

Yamaha hasn’t published a top speed in the specifications, but the NMAX E’s A1 classification puts it in the same general category as 125cc combustion scooters rather than urban mopeds.

Power comes from a centrally mounted 3.5 kWh lithium-ion battery, which Yamaha says provides up to 104 km (65 miles) of range on the WMTC Class 1 testing cycle. The L-shaped battery is mounted low and centrally in the chassis to help maintain a low center of gravity.

Unlike many electric scooters that rely on removable batteries, the NMAX E uses a fixed pack. Yamaha has compensated for that with an onboard 800W charger, allowing riders to plug the scooter directly into a household outlet or an AC Type 2 public charging station. A full 0-100% charge takes around 5.5 hours.

Riders can choose between three riding modes. Sport (S) mode offers the quickest acceleration, Touring (T) provides smoother power delivery for everyday riding and carrying a passenger, and Eco (E) reduces acceleration and top speed while maximizing range. Regenerative braking is also included.

The rest of the scooter is fairly well equipped, including traction control, ABS, 245mm front and rear disc brakes, 13-inch wheels, a 33mm fork, dual rear shocks, and even a reverse mode to make low-speed maneuvering easier.

Nice, the Nmax has always been the premium scoot we try to get when traveling in southeast asia. Always felt like it would've been even better electrified. No removable battery seems a bit of a miss. That might constrain a big chunk of demand.

A five-inch TFT display includes smartphone connectivity through Yamaha’s Motor On app, providing turn-by-turn navigation as well as battery status, ride information, maintenance reminders, and other connected features. There’s also keyless ignition, USB-C charging, LED lighting, and illuminated underseat storage large enough for a full-face helmet, depending on its size.

Perhaps most importantly, the NMAX E looks like a proper Yamaha scooter rather than an electric experiment. Its dual headlights and distinctive side panels closely follow the styling language of Yamaha’s existing MAX family.

That could prove important as established motorcycle manufacturers increasingly attempt to bring electric models into their existing lineups rather than treating them as separate curiosities.

Pricing and exact market availability haven’t yet been announced, but Yamaha is positioning the NMAX E as a 2027 model for the European market.

#4666. How do octopuses squeeze through tiny holes?

Published Nov 5, 2026 4:00 PM EST

Octopuses are famous for navigating their way through a tight squeeze. Even among invertebrates, their ability to compress themselves into seemingly impossibly tiny passageways is an impressive sight. But for years, marine biologists have remained perplexed by how these cephalopods routinely manage their maneuvers.

“There is no information about how octopuses squeeze through an opening far smaller than [their] body diameter,” Wenci Xin, a marine biologist at the National University of Singapore, said in a statement.

Xin and her colleagues recently provided Mayan octopuses (Octopus maya) and young common octopuses (Octopus vulgaris) with a chance to show off their skills. Their findings, published in a study today in the Journal of Experimental Biology, show that there may not necessarily be a “one size fits all” approach for octopuses.

First, the team needed some measurements. Previously, researchers assumed that an octopus’ stiff cranial case of cartilage that protects its central nervous system also dictates the limits of how small it can scrunch. Knowing this, Xin measured the distance between each specimen’s eyes to approximate the cartilage sheath’s width. In this case, the space between each octopus’ eyes ranged between about 0.6 and 1.3 inches wide.

The team then constructed customized, clear plastic aquarium boxes linked by holes either slightly larger or smaller than width between each set of octopus eyes. From there, they simply set up cameras, and let the cephalopods do their thing.

When encountering a comparatively large hole, each octopus initially prodded the opening with its arms before passing one limb through the hole. Usually, this was one of its two left front arms. It then slipped as many as five more arms through the portal, only to reach back with two of those limbs and use their suckers to stick to the initial box’s walls. Finally, they extended and stiffened these arms to push against the wall and maneuver the remaining limbs, mantle, and head through the hole. On average, an octopus successfully transitioned between boxes within about 20 seconds.

However, the octopuses often changed their approach when facing narrower holes often. The tighter squeeze limited how many arms an octopus could simultaneously thread through the opening. In these instances, the animals divided their final shimmying stage into two phases—first pulling all of its remaining arms through the hole, then compressing its mantle and scooting the rest of its body through the entry.

Well, only the common octopuses managed this. Xin’s team was surprised to learn the Mayan octopuses had no interest in the narrower holes. Instead, they simply hung out in another corner of the box without even testing the opening with their arms. Only when offered a second, larger passage did they get curious. In those scenarios, they felt around the smaller entry before opting to go through the larger of the two holes.

Although their study only focused on two species, their results indicate octopuses may vary in the ways they navigate tight spaces. At the same time, it appears their cranial cartilage may dictate at least some of their physical limitations. In any case, the biologists’ trials indicate that if an octopus at least thinks it can fit through an opening, it will certainly give it a try.

#4665. This California Tuning Shop Built an Insane Lexus GX–Toyota Tacoma Off-Road Pickup Truck

The “Lexus TX1” is equal parts GX 550, Taco, and trophy truck.

The Toyota Tacoma is one of the most popular mid-size pickup trucks on sale in America today, with a wide range of variants. But what if there were a luxury version? What if it were built by Lexus? California tuning shop Meso Customs has brought an answer to that line of questioning with its 2026 SEMA Show build, and the results are surprisingly compelling. It’s called the Lexus TX1, and it is immediately recognizable as the forbidden love child of a Lexus GX 550 and a fourth-generation Toyota Tacoma.

As Toyota’s luxury wing, Lexus does not have a pickup in its lineup; premium trucks tend to sell best when they have non-luxury badges. That said, the TX1 features horizontal grille slats and a prominent silver Lexus badge that somehow all seem to blend in and work together well. On top of all that, a rally-style light bar on top of the windshield and a high-clearance metal front bumper show the TX1 means business.

The project started as a CGI rendering, according before evolving into a full build a year later, with Meso Customs using CAD designs and fabricated individual pieces to make the TX1 a reality. But this isn’t a simple body kit build, either. The Yuba City, California-based shop added a lift kit from King Off-Road Racing Shocks, 74Weld portal axles, and 38-inch Toyo Tires.

The rear end is equally stunning, with a straight-across LED light bar from the GX550 and a tucked bumper. The bed was actually custom-built to incorporate the shape of a GX hatch into the Tacoma shell, while Baja Designs lights were integrated underneath and to the side of the wing mirrors. Meso Customs even displayed the TX1 with a color-matched Honda Grom in the bed, to show just how practical a Lexus pickup truck could be.

Of course, the TX1 build was not officially sponsored by Toyota or Lexus, so don’t expect a luxury-style Tacoma derivative from the Japanese automaker anytime soon. Even so, the idea that Lexus could build a proper off-road pickup with a luxurious interior is one fun fantasy. And if you’re inclined to see it in person, Meso Customs currently has the Lexus TX1 on display at the Toyo Tires Treadpass exhibit at the 2026 SEMA Show.

#4664. Inside the persistent myth that giant pandas are bad at sex

Published Nov 5, 2026 5:00 PM EST

Excerpted from INTHE COMPANY OF PANDAS: My Life with the World’s Favorite Bear by Dr. Brandie Smith. Copyright 2026 © by Dr. Brandie Smith. Reprinted by permission of Atria Books, an Imprint of Simon & Schuster, LLC.

WHEN YOU take care of pandas, your primary responsibility is to make more pandas. I was told point-blank during my interviews to become curator, “Your job is to get the panda pregnant.” I had a PhD in population genetics, and while I’d picked up considerable experience with endangered-species reproduction at the theoretical level, my hands-on experience was limited. But nothing helps you adapt quickly to a new job like being asked to help the world’s most famous bear survive as a species.

When I arrived at the National Zoo, it had been almost three years since the birth of Mei Xiang and Tian Tian’s first cub, Tai Shan. There are usually two years between births, so the mood at the zoo was not worried, but determined. I was added to the weekly panda meeting, which included the curator, keepers, veterinarians, scientists, and even the zoo’s director—at the time I started it was John Berry, but segued to Dennis Kelly in 2010—as we pored over every detail of the breeding and birthing plans, making micro adjustments, to ensure not just a successful fertilization, but that Mei Xiang had everything an expectant panda mother needed to be happy. It was as if we could group-project a healthy cub into existence. And although I understood the intense desire to see a panda cub, I quickly learned the interest focuses not just on the offspring, but includes the reproductive act itself. And that level of detailed attention was not just for the panda professionals, but for the hobbyists as well. I think of pandas as being more adorable than alluring, but for some reason, a great many people are obsessed with their sex lives.

In 1972, when President Nixon contacted The Washington Star to share the news that Ling-Ling and Hsing-Hsing would be coming to the capital, he told the reporter, “The problem, however, with pandas is that they don’t know how to mate.” Director Ted Reed was aware of the “sex problem” and determined to get ahead of it. As part of the preparations for the pandas’ arrival, even though the pair were still too young to breed, he hired the zoo’s first female scientist, Devra Kleiman, as a reproductive zoologist. Over the years, he wrote frequently to Smithsonian Secretary S.Dillon Ripley about the zoo’s efforts to breed the animals and wryly acknowledged his unusual fixation. Reed saw the yearslong failure not just as his own (especially after optimistically promising baby pandas for the bicentennial year in 1976) but even more generally as a “defeat for machismo; an utter humiliation for all zoo males.” That these two very dignified men were sending letters back and forth in which the director referred to himself as the Smithsonian’s “resident sex maniac,” and, later, how he regretted that “the great panda sex orgy of 1979” had not materialized, was not at all inappropriate.

Talking about sex is necessary for the people responsible for breeding endangered species, especially when you’re talking about the important work of making more pandas. When it comes to pandas, it seems that everyone’s inhibitions fall away. Other species don’t get that pass. At the zoo, we see parents’ natural modesty kick in as they describe an elephant’s erection as an extra tail or leg, or they rush their children past a pair of amorous orangutans that are “just playing.” But when it comes to pandas, even if the animals are in the midst of attempting the act, a wide swath of the public, including families, will line up to watch and cheer them on.

Maybe it’s because they’re so cute that they seem more pure than prurient. I think most of our preoccupation with the sex lives of giant pandas derives from the urban legend that, when it comes to the basics of reproduction, these bears are completely clueless. This is demonstrably false because modern pandas, Ailuropoda melanoleuca, and their precursors have been on the planet for millions of years. In the wild, the panda lifespan is roughly fifteen to twenty years, so if you do the math, you can see that it took a lot of successful panda procreation to carry the species into the twenty-first century. So, where did this idea originate? And why does it persist?

In the Company of Pandas: Exploring the Secrets of the World’s Favorite Bear by Dr. Brandie Smith is available wherever books are sold on November 10.

Dr. Brandie Smith is the John and Adrienne Mars Director of the Smithsonian’s National Zoo and Conservation Biology Institute. With decades of experience in animal care, conservation, and zoo management, she has overseen critical breeding programs for endangered species and has personally witnessed some of the most dramatic moments in panda conservation history at one of America’s premier zoos. Originally from Indiana, Pennsylvania, she grew up around animals and began her professional career as an intern at the Pittsburgh Zoo and the National Zoo.

#4663. Mercedes CTO: Level 3 Autonomy Ambitions Were ‘Early,’ Focus Turns to Level 2++

The new S-Class sets back the self-driving clock a little, but that might not be such a bad thing.

Mercedes-Benz’s autonomy roadmap has been a bit jumbled as of late. It was well over three years ago that the company’s Level 3 Drive Pilot automated driving system was approved to operate in Nevada, making it the first Level 3 system available in the U.S.

Those were exciting times on the surface, but with a hard speed limit of about 40 mph, the actual use case of the system wasn’t so great for American roads. A couple of years have since gone by from when Drive Pilot launched on the EQS and S-Class, so one might expect that Mercedes has taken those years to expand the system’s capability to higher speeds. That’s not exactly what’s been happening, though. Instead, the refreshed S-Class launched this year without Level 3 Drive Pilot capability at all. So, what gives?

In a recent media roundtable, Mercedes-Benz CTO Jörg Burzer explained how Mercedes’s thinking has evolved. “Level 3 ... so, what we did is, we were the first ones bringing Level 3 on the street in the U.S. and in Germany,” Burzer started. “And sometimes if you are too early, then you see that you have to work on what the customer really wants. And the challenge we had is facing the usability of the system.”

Rolling out a Level 3 highway system that was only capable of working at speeds typically reserved for urban streets, well, it sort of defeats the purpose. Yes, it was great for traffic jams, but Mercedes itself admits this Level 3 system was just too early.

“And then obviously we realized that we have to expand the ODD [Operation Design Domain]. We have to make it faster and from the speed level, but also we worked on the sensor set, and we learned a lot,” Burzer said. “And this was then fitting into everything we do, our normal hands-free, with Level 2++ [autonomy].

What’s up with the “Level 2++” talk? It’s the small step back Mercedes is taking from Level 3. Arguably, the Level 2++ system shipping on the S-Class and more new Mercedes models will be more helpful than the Level 3 it offered previously. However, being Level 2, it puts the onus and responsibility of the car back on the driver behind the wheel. With the Drive Pilot’s Level 3 operation, you could legally text or otherwise be completely disengaged from the driving experience with it activated.

Being able to go hands-free on the highway at high speeds is a driver assistance feature offered by all sorts of automakers today. Burzer recognizes how important it is for Mercedes to be competitive in this market, hence the switch to an extremely capable Level 2 system. The real trick will be rolling out in the months ahead, as the “++” part of the system allows for true point-to-point autonomous navigation on city streets. You’ll still need to pay attention, but the car should be able to do most of the work for you.

That’s the level Mercedes intends to stay at until it cracks Level 4, too. Instead of ramping back up to Level 3, Burzer believes it’s best to skip all the way toward Level 4, where you’d be able to do anything in the driver’s seat. “So we have, in the S-Class, up to 27 sensors for Level 2++,” Burzer said. “With this experience, we basically also decided, let's go for Level 4.”

But it’ll be a long time before Level 4 autonomous driving is available on a Mercedes-Benz vehicle, Burzer says he believes. Sometime after 2030 is his current best prediction. And when it does arrive, expect the features to roll out slowly, with urban driving being the last to fully come online.

#4662. Hydroxyapatite toothpaste promises to better protect your teeth. Here’s what the science says.

Published Nov 6, 2026 8:49 AM EST

There’s a new kid on the block in the toothpaste aisle. Next to the usual fluoride formulas, another option has been appearing: hydroxyapatite toothpaste.

Hydroxyapatite is the same mineral found in tooth enamel, and some claim using hydroxyapatite toothpaste can help plug tiny cracks in your teeth. Many brands are touting the new toothpaste as an effective alternative to fluoride. But does it actually protect your teeth, or is it just another trendy wellness product? After speaking with several experts, it seems like hydroxyapatite toothpaste might be worth trying.

Hydroxyapatite is a mineral made mostly of calcium and phosphorus that naturally occurs in human bones and teeth. It’s the main mineral in tooth enamel, the hard outer coating that helps protect your teeth from damage.

“Enamel is the hardest substance in the human body, but it’s not invulnerable,” says Dr. Joachim Enax, a chemist and senior scientist at Dr. Kurt Wolff GmbH & Co. KG, which makes hydroxyapatite toothpastes. Acids from foods and from bacteria in the mouth can gradually dissolve minerals from the tooth surface. Toothpastes that contain hydroxyapatite are designed to put some of that mineral back and help repair very early enamel damage, Enax explains.

If you’ve looked at these products, you may have seen labels mentioning “nano-hydroxyapatite” or “micro-hydroxyapatite.” That refers to the size of the mineral particles in the toothpaste. “Nano crystals are very fine and microscopic. Micro-hydroxyapatite crystals are larger,” says Dr. Hardy Limeback, a professor emeritus in the faculty of dentistry at the University of Toronto, who has been critical of fluoride use.

Both nano- and micro-hydroxyapatite occur naturally—for example, in breast milk—and because they are chemically the same as the mineral in tooth enamel, “they are added to toothpaste to plug up micro cracks or etches on the tooth surface,” he explains.

Hydroxyapatite toothpaste is not actually new. In the 1960s, research at NASA on growing crystals for electronics led to a patent for repairing teeth by growing hydroxyapatite crystals. A Japanese company later acquired the patent and introduced the first hydroxyapatite-based toothpastes in the 1980s.

Since hydroxyapatite was approved as an anti-cavity ingredient in Japan in 1993, similar toothpastes have become available in Europe (since 2006) and Canada (since 2015).

In the United States, you can buy hydroxyapatite toothpastes online and in some stores, but neither the Food and Drug Administration nor the American Dental Association has approved hydroxyapatite as an anti-cavity ingredient. To earn the ADA’s Seal of Acceptance—an official indication that a toothpaste helps prevent cavities—a product must contain fluoride.

Hydroxyapatite toothpaste can help remineralize enamel that has been weakened by acids from dental plaque or acidic foods, say Limeback and Enax. By promoting remineralization and forming a protective layer that helps shield enamel from acids, it may also protect teeth against cavities, says Dr. Elżbieta Paszyńska, a dental surgeon and head of the department of integrated dentistry and endodontics at Poznan University of Medical Sciences in Poland.

Fluoride prevents cavities in a similar way: Fluoride ions are incorporated into the enamel’s structure, helping repair very early decay and making the enamel more resistant to acid over time.

Paszyńska’s group ran two randomized clinical trials at two medical universities, with nearly 200 participants each: one in children aged three to seven, and one in adults with healthy teeth. For 12 to 18 months, participants used either a hydroxyapatite or a fluoride toothpaste. (Both studies were funded by Dr. Kurt Wolff GmbH & Co. KG.)

“At the end of both studies, children and adults using the hydroxyapatite toothpaste were no more likely to develop new carious lesions than those using fluoride toothpaste,” she says. “These findings demonstrated, in two independent clinical trials, that hydroxyapatite toothpaste can provide caries [cavity] protection comparable to fluoride toothpaste in daily oral care.”

Hydroxyapatite toothpastes may also help reduce tooth sensitivity by physically filling and sealing exposed dentinal tubules (the tiny channels leading to tooth nerves), Limeback and Enax note. In one study, people who used a nano-hydroxyapatite toothpaste for two to four weeks were less sensitive to cold air and touch than they had been at the start.

Early studies—most conducted in laboratory settings—suggest that regular use of hydroxyapatite toothpastes can also have a whitening effect. The mineral can form a thin, white layer on the tooth surface that helps mask the yellow tones of the underlying dentin and reduce the appearance of stains.

“This is different from bleaching; it is about restoring and maintaining the natural appearance of enamel,” Enax says. But more clinical trials are needed to confirm this effect in people.

Why our ancestors had straight teeth without braces

Is crossing your eyes really bad for you? We asked an optometrist.

In Europe, health officials have closely studied nano-hydroxyapatite in toothpastes and mouthwashes. In July 2025, the Scientific Committee on Consumer Safety said this ingredient is safe in amounts up to about 30 percent in toothpaste and 10 percent in mouthwash. Most products on the market use 10 percent or less, which is well within that limit.

In the studies they reviewed, rod-shaped nano-hydroxyapatite did not damage DNA or harm cells, even when tested at high concentrations on mouth tissue samples in the lab. (The safety opinion does not apply to products that use needle-shaped particles.)

The committee concluded that any tiny amount of nano-hydroxyapatite particles that enter the cells lining the mouth is naturally removed from the body when those cells shed. If you swallow some toothpaste by accident, the particles are expected to break down quickly in stomach acid, causing no harmful effects.

Even with growing evidence in its favor, some U.S. dentists are cautious about swapping fluoride for hydroxyapatite.

“As far as telling someone, ‘Hey, stop using fluoride toothpaste and start using this,’ we don’t have enough evidence yet,” Dr. Hema Arany, a dentist and associate professor at the Medical University of South Carolina, said in a recent interview. “And so when it comes to standard of care, we are not recommending hydroxyapatite toothpaste.”

But some people avoid fluoride because they’re worried about possible links between fluoride and skin problems or neurodevelopmental issues in children, though these concerns remain debated and the data is still evolving. The World Health Organization and the American Dental Association maintain that fluoride toothpaste is safe and highly effective at preventing tooth decay when used as directed.

According to ethical guidance published in the Journal of the American Dental Association, for people who refuse to use fluoride, hydroxyapatite “is likely the second-best option.”

#4659. Inside Disney’s Animal Nutrition Center, which doles out 10,000 pounds of food every day

Published Nov 6, 2026 10:00 AM EST

Cases of peanut butter, bright red boxes of Shredded Wheat cereal, and so many varieties of tea that even Mary Poppins would be excited. Around the corner, large wooden crates teeming with wide leaves and sturdy grasses, and a walk-in refrigerator full of fresh produce sit ready to turn into dishes that are a feast for the eyes and the belly.

For the team working at Disney’s Animal Nutrition Center (ANC) at Walt Disney World Resort in Orlando, Florida, it’s like Thanksgiving every day. The roughly 40 cast members on the animal nutrition team is responsible for feeding the over 5,000 animals at Disney’s Animal Kingdom Theme Park and The Seas at EPCOT. It takes time, a devotion to the science of nutrition, and really knowing your audience to deliver about 10,000 pounds of food per day. And like putting together any big meal, it requires a team effort, which extends well beyond the animals at Disney.

“What we’re trying to do is provide the optimal nutrition for animals to live long and healthy lives, and we do that by taking information from a lot of different fields,” Animal Nutrition Operations Manager Dr. Heidi Bissell tells Popular Science. “From the field of agriculture, we learn a lot about animal physiology and how animals work, and can then design diets with the ingredients we have for specific purposes.”

In addition to bringing in knowledge from across different scientific disciplines, the team collaborates with other accredited zoos, aquariums, and universities to share research and data on animal nutrition. They’ve published studies on animals from bigger animals like zebras and rhinos, to smaller fish and amphibians, which is crucial to filling in nutritional gaps. If the team is not sure what a particular species needs to eat in order to thrive, they will turn to comparative nutrition for answers.

“We go with a close relative [and] take what we know about the animals we do know a lot about and apply that to some of our other species,” Bissell explains. “Then we learn from our own animals by assessing how they’re doing on the diets that we’re offering, so we can gauge their nutritional status and make adjustments as needed.”

Staying nimble and making these adjustments is also important. If a supply chain issue disrupts what the nutrition team can get, having a back-up plan that includes nutritious food is critical. If an animal is familiar and comfortable with at least a few types of food, they will generally fare better, whether there are shortages or not.

At the same time, the nutrition team works to ensure that the food and its presentation mimics life in the wild as much as possible.

“Animals in the wild are spending their days solving puzzles, trying to figure out how to eat, while staying away from predators or toxins,” Bissell says. “They’re making a lot of decisions all day, so if we just offered them food in a bowl that would not provide them with mental stimulation.”

One of the most common behaviors is foraging, or digging through obstacles like grass, mud, or leaves to find food. The dishes the team creates are often presented in a way that encourages foraging, so that the animals keep up those natural behaviors. Leaves will be hung up in a tree for the giraffes to eat as they would in the wild. Carnivores like lions will get whole prey and bones to eat, which also helps keep their own jaws and teeth healthy. The team also pays attention to seasonal shifts to keep animals in their natural rhythm.

“Probably the biggest group of animals that we do this with would be birds,” says Bissell. “If they’re laying eggs, they might need more calcium, so we might add sources of calcium into their diet.”

Surprisingly, feeding bigger animals like lions and elephants is not as challenging as making sure that the insectivores have enough to eat. True to their name, anteaters almost exclusively eat bugs, and can consume up to 3,000 insects per day. To keep up with all of those the bugs, Bissell and the team work side-by-side with manufacturers to ensure their insect pellets meet the physical and nutritional standards needed to align with insects the anteaters encounter in the wild. To supplement, the anteaters will also get a bit of produce with the insects, since they do also eat fruit.

“We do a lot with like ice cakes, where we can freeze food in blocks of ice and can color the water with like vegetable dyes, so it’s fun and engaging. And the ice, especially in Florida in the summer, is really nice for hydration,” Bissell explains. “We are often pulling from what’s already in the animal diet or similar things, because just like humans, it’s not a great idea to just add a bunch of stuff on top of your existing diet.”

They’ll also follow themes, from a little fall pies to a driver’s license out of fruit and leaves for a gorilla’s 16th birthday and a food sculpture shaped like a margarita for a 21st birthday. That devotion to keeping meals fresh and creative helps all animals, humans included.

“I like making animals’ lives better, and by extension people’s lives better, because we care about these animals so much,” says Bissell.

#4658. The 2027 Mercedes-AMG GT 63 4-Door Coupe Turns a New Page for AMG

An EV that sounds, and often feels, like it has been inspired by AMG’s V-8-powered past.

The 2027 Mercedes-AMG GT 63 4-Door Coupe marks an entirely new era for AMG. There isn’t a lick of hardware shared between this electric performance sedan and the milquetoast AMG EVs that came before it. The same goes for its drive software, which is as equally important as the exotic electric powertrain hiding under the car’s polarizing metal and LEDs. More than anything, this car is a statement to the world that Mercedes and AMG mean business in the cutthroat world of rapidly evolving electric performance.

It is familiar to AMG’s combustion offerings on purpose. Twist the dial over to Sport+ on the steering wheel, and the most convincing engine and transmission simulation in an EV yet comes to life. There’s no blend between electric motor and gasoline sounds to be heard here. It’s the twin-turbo 4.0-liter V-8 from the previous-generation AMG GT R Coupe, and it’s quite the circus act.

Mercedes calls it AMGFORCE Sport+ (a terrible name), and engineers took over 100 measurements with 16 microphone positions that allowed software gurus to reconstruct the sound digitally. What makes it convincing isn’t the sound, though. Mercedes uses the Burmester 4D sound exciters in the seats that produce vibrations with music to replicate the vibration and harshness you’d feel if a real V-8 were running up and down its rev range. You have to surrender your brain to the simulation, but if you do, it works. I was cackling in the driver’s seat all day, but you can just as easily turn off the fun and games for a pure EV soundscape.

Like other systems that do the same (see the Hyundai Ioniq 5 and the Genesis GV60), the AMG multiclutch transmission is fully simulated too. With a “redline” at 7200 rpm, the car lets you manually shift through seven speeds via steering-wheel-mounted paddles. Downshifts are accompanied with realistic engine braking on the overrun. Sadly, you can’t bang it off a simulated rev limiter at the top of each “gear,” but it’s still a hoot. If there’s a downside to this system, it’s the fake noise being piped to the outside world. Similar to Dodge’s cringey Fratzonic exhaust, Mercedes uses an exterior speaker system to project V-8 sounds from the rear of the car. Once the myth is busted, this is not convincing anybody and is likely to make a driver the butt of many a joke at the local Cars & Coffee.

V-8 clone technology aside, the AMG GT 63 4-Door Coupe produces numbers that should make even the staunchest of doubters raise an eyebrow in interest. Three axial flux motors—two in the rear and one in front—engineered with YASA combine to produce 1153 hp and 1475 lb-ft of torque. That peak power is accomplished in either Race or Boost mode, but don’t fret about it being temporary. Boost mode lasts a wild 63 seconds should you want it, and AMG says it could truly continue for as long as you desire in Race with zero derating. Standard, continuous output in other modes sits at 711 hp.

My first drive was at the gorgeous Ascari racetrack in southern Spain. It’s the ideal place to test out the car’s claimed 0–60-mph time of 2.3 seconds, and while I didn’t come close to the electronically limited 186-mph top speed, its rapid pull up to and beyond 130 mph suggests the limiter won’t take too long to reach.

There are several keys to this big sedan’s ability to run lap after lap at the track. One is direct oil cooling for the motors and gearsets, this using a proprietary, secret oil. Next, Mercedes uses water-cooled silicon carbide inverters. And finally, the most important piece is the 106-kWh, 800-volt AMG High Performance Electric Battery. This battery pack was developed specifically for AMG models (it won’t be used elsewhere) and uses unique cells with electrically nonconducting cooling oil flowing around each one.

The thermal management going on here is second to none, and on top of the track performance, it enables DC fast-charging at speeds beyond 600 kilowatts. That’s faster than any other EV on sale in America today. No, there aren’t any charging stations in the U.S. to support that madness, but Mercedes wheeled out a charger for a demonstration at Ascari, and I witnessed speeds of over 630 kilowatts. The claim is 10–80 percent in only 11 minutes, and given the right charger, this car can make that happen.

Lots of power doesn’t necessarily make a great EV, but that’s where AMG’s software wizards come into play. This tri-motor setup is truly only as competent as the software that’s running it, because there isn’t a single center differential or torque-vectoring diff to be found. Mercedes installed three completely independent electric motors with an absurd amount of torque and then went about making that controllable. Engineers tell me repeatedly that among the challenges, dialing in the proper drive characteristics was the biggest of all.

Funnily enough, this newfound flexibility in the powertrain led AMG to develop a set of dials with nine settings each it calls “AMG Race Engineer.” The Response Control dial lets you change throttle sensitivity, ranging from entirely dull to jumpy on the high end. A Traction Control dial does exactly what you’d expect, with one ensuring the car won’t slip an inch and nine turning the car into a full-on drift machine—there’s a Drift mode that shuts off the front motor too. Last, and most intriguing, there’s Agility Control. In practice, it’s like having an infinitely adjustable yaw controller at your beck and call. At one, it’s all understeer as you brake and steer into a corner. Dial it up to around the five-to-seven range, and the AMG transforms into a car with shockingly neutral balance, letting me induce just enough oversteer to coax the rear into a corner as I trail it in. Go all the way to nine, and you better watch yourself with how much the rear is going to be moving.

I’ve never driven a car that can behave so differently from corner to corner simply at the twist of a dial, but that’s the kind of freedom afforded by three extremely powerful, independent electric motors. When asked how the magic happens, engineers rattle on about how they’ve simulated differentials just by using positive and negative motor torque. Sometimes the car will be using brake regeneration at specific corners to induce the behavior you’ve selected; other times traditional brake torque vectoring intrudes to pinch the calipers to control the car’s movements. It all sounds like an impossible orchestra to compose, and yet somehow, they nailed it. All the way down to the adjustable traction control that lets you choose just how sideways you want to get accelerating out of a corner. Lock it down for safety, or send plumes of smoke into the air. The choice is genuinely entirely yours.

After a few laps of getting acclimated to how all these systems interact, I started to understand this big four-door’s personality. Around a racetrack, it drives similar to a Porsche Taycan that doesn’t take life so seriously. Or in other words, it drives how you’d expect an AMG product to, safely sliding around and roaring its V-8 trumpet.

The 63 comes with AMG’s Ride Control air suspension with active roll stabilization that uses the same hydraulically interconnected dampers as you’d find on the AMG GT 63 Coupe, allowing chassis engineers to delete the anti-roll bars. I didn’t drive the 63 on the road, but the ride over curbing was considerably better than I expected from a 5534-pound performance sedan that corners as flat as it does. Active aero in the form of underbody Venturi flow elements, a deployable rear spoiler, an extendable rear diffuser, and front cooling louvers keep the car in either the most advantageous aerodynamic profile for range or in maximum-downforce-and-stability mode.

The brakes are mighty, with carbon-ceramic rotors up front and steel rotors in the rear. Huge recuperation capability from the axial-flux electric motors means they don’t even have to work very hard. Despite eight laps around Ascari, there was hardly a whiff of brake smell when I pulled back into pit lane—yet another shock for a large and heavy EV. Unfortunately, brake feel is a sore point, with the pedal offering an airy sensation through the first half before firming up toward the bottom of the stroke. Braking distances seem comparable to other large performance sedans in practice, in part due to the Michelin Pilot Sport S 5 tires Mercedes fits. More aggressive Cup 2 tires would take this car to another level, but it’s a step engineers were hesitant to take with this model, perhaps saving the grippier rubber for a more extreme version to come.

My other biggest gripe: The fake V-8 and transmission disappear in Race mode. Outside of Sport+, this EV accelerates and sounds like any other megaquick electric car. It’s unending, brutal, and, eventually, a bit boring. Thankfully, the slidetastic chassis keeps things entertaining on the racetrack, though I suspect the number of owners who bring this beast to the track will be in the double digits at best. You can technically bring it there and pound around with none of the typical downsides of pushing an EV, but this AMG is no track star.

The AMG GT 63 4-Door Coupe starts at $176,500, which sure sounds high, but at the same time reasonable with how much effort AMG put into this car from a hardware, software, and material perspective. It’s also right in line with a Porsche Taycan Turbo, the GT 63’s closest competitor.

If you’re inclined to such an experience in an EV, there’s no better internal-combustion simulator in existence. Combine this party trick with the infinitely adjustable handling attitude, and you’re left looking at a technological fortress of performance. It’s one hell of a statement. I’m just not sure many people are going to be willing to listen to it.

#4657. Maximo milestone: friendly robot has completed 300,000 tasks

After completing the first half of Amazon’s Bellefield complex last summer, Maximo engineers have put their helpful robot friend into high gear, with the latest version 3.0 robot-equipped construction crews installing as many as 24 solar panel modules per hour, per person. And now, the company is reporting that Maximo has completed its 300,000th construction task. (!)

If that 24 modules per hour, per person rate sounds fast, that’s because it is. At full tilt, the latest Maximo robot-equipped crews have nearly doubled the output of traditional installation methods at similar solar locations throughout Southern California. Now, with 300,000 tasks under its belt, the robot is proving to be both fast and durable.

“The future of solar construction depends on bringing together the experience of our people and new technology,” explains Matt Tetrault, President of Primoris’ Renewables business.

Like just about everyone these days, Maximo is playing up its machines’ NVDIVIA hardware, re-branding its robots’ repetitive automation as “physical AI.” That’s not to say the robots don’t work, however – as their deployment at Amazon’s Bellefield solar field is proving.

(By) leveraging NVIDIA AI infrastructure together with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries and NVIDIA Isaac Sim open robotics simulation framework, the Maximo team was able to develop, test and refine robotic capabilities through physics-based simulation and AI driven modeling before deploying updates in the field. The combination of AI, vision, robotics and simulation driven engineering reduced development and validation timelines and increased confidence in field performance as the robotic fleet scaled.

Amazon Web Services (AWS) powered the development, deployment, and operation of Maximo’s AI-driven field systems. AWS provides scalable computing, automated software delivery, and advanced data analytics, including real-time construction intelligence, enabling Maximo to collect operational robotics data and continuously improve performance.

The rapid deployment of solar panels at utility scale projects like this one, which is set to eventually reach over a GW of solar generating capacity, will help companies like Amazon reduce their carbon footprint, of course – but also save them big money as the price of fossil fuels continues to climb.

So Primoris’ Renewables is the name of a business, Maximo is the name of a solar robotics company incubated by The AES Corporation. Maximo makes a robot (also called Maximo I think) using NVDIVIA hardware and software, and also AWS cloud software, and Bellefield is a solar field owned by Amazon. Or so I gather so far.

The Maximo team says it has plans to extend its robots potential use cases beyond solar and into construction tasks that require similar pick and place and feeding and attaching movements, site logistics, and site cleanup. And like just about every other business that demands a high degree of physical labor, the construction industry is facing huge labor shortages, making machines like Maximo that provide real efficiency gains welcome additions to the job site.

#4656. NASA teases experimental X-70 ‘Fractal’ aircraft

Published Nov 6, 2026 11:00 AM EST

NASA has unveiled its next experimental aircraft, dubbed the X-70 Fractal. Well, “unveiled” may be a bit of a stretch. During this week’s UP.Summit at Kennedy Space Center in Florida, NASA administrator Jared Isaacman announced plans for the “crewed, high-performance platform” designed to boost maneuverability, flight control, and “other cutting-edge technologies in real flight.”

Beyond that, you’re guess is probably about as good as anyone’s. Even X-70’s sole visual hint may mean nothing at all. The shadowy frame seen silhouetted by fog in NASA’s announcement is explicitly identified as AI “generated content.” This means even the rounded cockpit, splayed tail fins, and extended wings may ultimately not even show up in the final design.

Despite a lack of photographs, NASA did provide some more concrete details about the X-70. The aircraft will have a 10,000 pound takeoff weight and will cruise at Mach .75 (about 570 miles per hour) at a maximum altitude of 45,000 feet. Its operational range is also expected to exceed 1,500 nautical miles (1,726 miles).

“For decades, NASA Aeronautics has used X-planes to develop technologies that advance aviation,” NASA Research and Technology Mission Directorate director Laurie Grindle said in the agency’s announcement. “It’s exciting to bring on another X-plane to accelerate and drive aeronautics research.”

NASA also emphasized the X-70’s modular construction, which will allow quick swaps of internal and external payloads. As The War Zone noted, these features are likely intended to facilitate tests of experimental autonomous deployments and drone technology. The X-70 may also feature “bleeding-edge” abilities like morphing wings and “air-burst” controls, which allow aircraft to precisely maneuver midflight solely through blasts of pressurized air.

Isaacman said he expects the X-70 to complete its first flight within the next two years, although it’s always useful to take experimental aircraft timelines with a grain of salt. When NASA awarded Lockheed Martin the contract to develop its X-59 aircraft in 2016, the aim was to have a vehicle ready for testing by 2020. The actual X-59’s maiden flight ultimately took place on October 28, 2025.

#4655. Range Rover Replacing Evoque and Velar Models with Upcoming GT EV

It’s unclear if either SUV will have a 2027 model year run in the U.S. market.

Prepare to say goodbye to Range Rover’s two most affordable models, as the Evoque and Velar celebrate their final model year in production. The company has confirmed to British outlet Autocar that the volume sellers will cease production after 2027 and be replaced by the new Range Rover GT.

“Both Range Rover Velar and Range Rover Evoque will continue to be sold in selected global markets where demand remains strong, throughout 2027,” a JLR spokesperson told Car and Driver. “Production of both models will end in mid-2027 in line with their natural product lifecycles, as JLR’s manufacturing facilities transition to build its next generation of vehicles.”

See all results for Land Rover Range Rover Evoque for sale near 07011

The Evoque and Velar’s sales have accounted for just 6000 of Land Rover’s U.S. sales through this year. Paltry numbers, representing only 10 percent of the brand’s 2026 sales volume in the U.S. so far. It would not surprise us if North America is not one of the global markets the company considers a high-demand market for these two models. We asked for clarification from JLR but have not heard back.

The two SUVs are attractive not only for their styling but also for their relatively low prices compared with the six-figure ask for the flagship Range Rover SUV. The Evoque starts at around $52,000 and the Velar at around $64,000. The Evoque rides on the same platform as the Land Rover Discovery Sport SUV, which was discontinued after the 2026 model year.

The move comes amid a broader strategy shift at JLR, Jaguar and Land Rover’s parent company. In the past year, both brands have focused on launching electric-powered flagships, the most buzzworthy of which is the Jaguar Type 01 sedan.

Range Rover has launched the Range Rover Electric and is preparing a Range Rover Sport Electric, effectively electrifying its core lineup. A new entry-level Range Rover GT is also on the way and will effectively replace the Evoque and Velar once it hits production as a 2028 model.

Like the Jaguar Type 01, the Range Rover GT takes the shape of a long and low sedan-like vehicle with a minimalist interior and an all-wheel-drive electric powertrain. The Range Rover GT will launch first as an EV, but the company says the platform is capable of hosting gas and hybrid powertrains as well. A starting price of around $90,000 is expected, significantly increasing the entry price to the Range Rover brand.

See all results for Land Rover Range Rover Evoque for sale near 07011

Land Rover’s other two brands—Defender and Discovery—are expected to pick up the slack and serve customers in the sub-$90,000 price range once the Evoque and Velar cease production. A Defender Sport model is reportedly in the works as a junior entry to the popular Defender off-roader. It stands to reason that a Discovery Sport model could be revived in the future, possibly as an EV, to serve as an entry point to the Discovery lineup.

#4654. Former CAKE team is back in the kitchen with a new electric motorcycle

If the new ReBake Abler electric motorcycle looks like it might share a bit of DNA with Sweden’s dearly departed CAKE, there’s a good reason for that.

ReBake Motors has officially unveiled its first electric two-wheeler at EICMA 2026 in Milan, introducing the Abler as a highly modular, utility-focused electric moped and light motorcycle.

Behind the new Swedish company is founder and CEO Karl Ytterborn, who spent eight years at CAKE from its founding in 2016 through 2024. CAKE famously built some of the most interesting minimalist electric motorcycles and utility bikes on the market before ultimately collapsing after failing to secure additional funding. Ytterborn says ReBake is intended to apply many of the lessons learned during that experience, while eliminating unnecessary cost and complexity.

Its chunky 42mm aluminum tube frame isn’t just a styling exercise. ReBake designed it as a mounting system, allowing cargo accessories to attach directly to the frame at multiple locations. That means riders can configure the bike for everything from carrying groceries and passengers to more serious utility duties.

There are two versions. The Abler45 is an EU L1e-B moped with a 45 km/h (28 mph) top speed, 4 kW nominal motor and 5.12 kW peak output. It starts at €3,990 including VAT.

The €4,990 Abler80 steps up to the A1 light motorcycle category, increasing nominal power to 6.14 kW and peak power to 7.68 kW while pushing the top speed beyond 80 km/h (50 mph). Both versions use a direct-drive rear hub motor.

Energy comes from removable 2 kWh lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries weighing 17 kg (37.5 lb) apiece. The Abler45 comes standard with one battery but can carry two, while the Abler80 includes two for 4 kWh of total capacity. With both batteries, ReBake claims up to 160 km (99 miles) of low-speed urban range on the Abler45 or 114 km (71 miles) on the Abler80. Each battery can be charged either on or off the bike from a normal 230V outlet, reaching a full charge in four hours.

The rest of the hardware includes 14-inch cast wheels, 140mm of front suspension travel, dual rear shocks, front and rear disc brakes with combined braking, regenerative braking, and full LED lighting.

Perhaps more interesting than any individual specification, though, is simply seeing another Swedish electric motorcycle startup emerge from CAKE’s ashes.

CAKE demonstrated that there was plenty of appetite for unconventional, lightweight electric motorcycles. Unfortunately, it also demonstrated just how difficult it is to turn that enthusiasm into a sustainable business.

ReBake appears to be getting another crack at that equation – this time with eight years’ worth of lessons already baked in.

#4653. Baby whale surprises scientists

Published Nov 6, 2026 11:33 AM EST

The 2027 North Atlantic right whale (Eubalaena glacialis) baby season has officially begun. The calving season lasts from November through April, and is a particularly important stretch of time given that the species is classified as critically endangered by the IUCN Red List.

Due to their low numbers, scientists are closely monitoring these baleen whales. Yet even with all of that surveillance, one whale managed to keep a secret up until September.Experts spotted a known female and her previously unidentified calf from last calving season near Anticosti Island, Quebec, Canada, according to the New England Aquarium.

The 38-year-old female right whale is called Silt. In addition to being a mother, Silt is  also a grandmother and great-grandmother. The new calf is her sixth baby known to scientists.

“Silt managed to fly under the radar of survey teams throughout the spring and summer,” according to the aquarium “Although we don’t know exactly when or where her calf was born, she was briefly seen in the southeastern United States calving grounds in February, so it’s possible the calf was born there.”

More North Atlantic right whales are always good news. They are one of the most endangered large whales, and are vulnerable to ship collisions and fishing gear entanglement. Almost exactly a year ago, we were happy to report that the species is showing signs of slowly rebounding. 2024’s estimate of around 384 North Atlantic right whales represents a 2.1 percent increase from 2023’s estimate.

“The population increase is really good news, and so far, what we’ve seen in 2025 is also good news,” New England Aquarium senior scientist Heather Pettis told Popular Science in October 2025 . But “we’re talking about a population of 384 individual whales—that’s still incredibly low,” she added. “Yes, we’re seeing increases. They’re small, and we still are seeing injuries to animals from human activities. And so, you know, I say that we’re cautiously optimistic.”

#4652. Florida Man Who Allegedly Stole $210,000 Porsche Panamera Apparently Forgot He Was Wearing a GPS Ankle Monitor

A previous police chase had earned the 19-year-old suspect a tracking device, which investigators say placed him at the scene of the Porsche theft.

We at Road & Track certainly don't know if a handbook for car thieves exists. But if it did, there would certainly have to be a chapter on how to avoid getting caught. And that chapter probably begins with some fairly obvious advice—like, for example, don't steal a $210,000 Porsche Panamera while wearing a GPS ankle monitor that tells the authorities exactly where you are.

According to a report by WPLG Local 10 News, 19-year-old Joseph Dexter Watson IV has been accused by authorities of participating in the October 24 theft of a Porsche Panamera. The luxury car was reportedly stolen from a multimillion-dollar mansion in Miami-Dade County's Horse Country neighborhood.

According to investigators, Watson and at least three accomplices arrived at the property in a Mercedes-Benz shortly before 6:30 p.m. The group allegedly broke into a Cadillac Escalade parked outside the gated property, but apparently not satisfied with the score, one of the suspects reportedly climbed over a fence and stole the Porsche. Inside the Panamera, authorities say, were seven pairs of shoes valued at roughly $4200. The Porsche's owner quickly tracked the car to a Hampton Inn parking lot in Deerfield Beach; When Broward Sheriff's Office deputies arrived, they found the Porsche, but nobody was inside.

However, locating one of the suspects was surprisingly easy. See, in January, Watson allegedly led police on a bizarre chase: according to authorities, the rented Kia he was driving crashed into a mail truck, when he then reportedly tried to hide in another mail truck before attempting to flee the scene in an Uber. Watson was caught and spent approximately two months in jail before being released on bond in March.

As a condition of his release, Watson was ordered to wear a GPS ankle monitor. According to investigators, it was that very monitor that placed him at the scene of the Porsche theft. He now faces new charges, including traveling with intent to commit burglary of an occupied dwelling, masked burglary of an occupied dwelling, and grand theft of a motor vehicle. He is being held at the Turner Guilford Knight Correctional Center—this time, without bond.

#4651. Tesla wins trade zone status for Texas Megapacks, but China tariffs stay

Tesla’s Megapack factory in Brookshire, Texas, is now officially a foreign-trade zone, a US customs program that lets manufacturers defer duties on imported parts. The FTZ Board’s approval, published in the Federal Register on Monday, runs for 14 months.

It’s easy to read this as Tesla getting a pass on tariffs for the Chinese LFP cells inside its Megapacks. Tesla’s own application says otherwise: parts hit by Section 301, 232, or 122 tariffs still pay them.

Tesla filed the request on May 20 for Subzone 84AM, part of FTZ 84 in the Houston area. That’s the factory where Tesla started Megapack 3 production in August, with a planned capacity of 50 GWh per year.

The application lists roughly 80 imported components Tesla wants to bring in under zone procedures, from coolant pumps and transformers to busbars, wiring harnesses, circuit boards and battery cells. Duty rates on those parts go up to 6.5%, while finished Megapacks and Bento inverters range from duty-free to 3.4%.

That gap is the usual reason companies set up an FTZ. A manufacturer in a zone can normally elect to pay the finished product’s lower rate instead of the rate on each imported part.

But the application spells out the limit. Components subject to duties under Section 122 of the Trade Act, Section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act, or Section 301 “require subject merchandise to be admitted to FTZs in privileged foreign status,” according to the notice.

Privileged foreign status locks in a part’s own classification and tariff treatment when it enters the zone. So a Chinese LFP cell that ends up in a Megapack sold in the US still pays the Section 301 tariff on Chinese non-EV lithium-ion batteries, which jumped from 7.5% to 25% on January 1, 2026. Tesla just pays it later, when the finished Megapack leaves the zone.

Here’s what Tesla actually gets out of it:

The approval came with the same wording the FTZ Board has used all year. Production was “authorized on a limited basis,” and “further subject to a fourteen-month time period.”

Tesla got an identical decision for Megapack and inverter production at Fremont, Livermore and Lathrop in California this summer, with a one-year limit instead. Eastman Chemical, battery pack maker Rose Batteries, and chipmaker Qorvo all received similar time-limited, “limited basis” approvals in 2026.

The 14-month clock puts the expiry around the end of 2027. That’s roughly when LG Energy Solution is due to start supplying Tesla with LFP cells from Michigan under a $4.3 billion contract for Megapack 3, with mass production expected in the second half of 2027.

Tesla hasn’t hidden the issue. When tariffs escalated in April 2025, CFO Vaibhav Taneja said the impact on energy storage would be “outsized since we source lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery cells from China.” We wrote at the time that Tesla’s only growing business was kneecapped by Trump’s tariffs.

Tesla has since brought up its own LFP cell factory in Nevada, but Taneja said it would only cover a fraction of Tesla’s installed capacity. And Brookshire alone is designed for 50 GWh a year, on top of the 40 GWh Lathrop factory in California.

Tesla’s Megapacks are bringing big batteries to the grid, but you can get the same benefits at home by pairing solar with storage. With electricity rates up almost 10% last year and expected to keep climbing, going solar is one of the best ways to protect yourself against rising costs. #4650. Scientists detect ‘pregnant’ coral using ultrasound device

Published Nov 6, 2026 12:47 PM EST

Scientists have a new tool in the fight to save Earth’s endangered coral reefs and it’s something many moms-to-be know all too well: the ultrasound.

This week, veteran camera-maker Canon announced its high-tech ultrasound platform can scan living coral submerged underwater and detect eggs developing inside them. Until now, checking whether coral was carrying eggs typically required cutting it open. This ultrasound development means researchers can assess coral reproduction non-invasively for the first time. By using ultrasound, scientists can gather crucial information about a coral’s reproductive health and try to predict when it will release its eggs. That insight can help conservationists time and target their restoration efforts without damaging or sacrificing the species in the process.

Canon conducted the experiment in collaboration with United Kingdom-based conservation organization Coral Spawning International (CSI). The team used Canon’s Aplio i700, an advanced medical ultrasound system normally used on humans in hospital settings. In this case though, it scanned six species of large polyp stony coral with varying skeletal structures. The device’s powerful mixture of high and ultra high frequency probes let researchers see through the coal’s skeletons and view their internal structures. The team verified their results by cutting open one coral species, Trachyphyllia geoffroyi, and taking high powered images of its interior. Those images were then cross referenced with the results from the ultrasound, confirming that the structure identified in the scan were indeed eggs.

“This experiment demonstrates that imaging innovation has the power to show us what was previously unseen, creating a deeper understanding of the world around us,” Canon EMEA Sustainability and Government Affairs Director Peter Bragg said in a statement. “By unlocking this knowledge, we hold a fundamental belief that imaging has the power to transform the world.”

Coal can use all the help it can get. Late last month, the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) released a sobering assessment warning that nearly all (96 percent) of the Earth’s coral reef ecosystem face an extremely high risk of collapse within the next 50 years. The main culprit? Warming oceans and heat waves brought on by climate change.

That dire threat isn’t just a problem for coral, either. Coral reefs, sometimes referred to as the “rainforests of the sea” are the among the most biodiverse eco systems on the planet and support an estimated quarter of all marine species. When reefs collapse, the coral dies and is replaced by algae and sponges which are not able to support as diverse a range of marine life. As a result, the ocean’s overall biological health ebbs and flows alongside coral.

Understanding when corals will spawn can give scientists critical data for breeding and a leg up on restoration efforts, which can help them try and tip the odds in  coral’s favor. Ultrasound scans could make that work more precise while sparing the coral from an untimely dissection.

#4649. The Toyota Supra and BMW Z4 Are Officially Sold Out: Report

Production for the sibling sports car pair has ended, and the last units in the U.S. have, apparently, left dealer lots.

When BMW and Toyota first joined forces to reimagine two iconic sports car nameplates—the Supra and the Z4—the collaboration was a surprise, but also turned out to be quite a success, at least in terms of the smiles both cars delivered. Six years later, Toyota and BMW are sunsetting production of the sibling sports cars, and shoppers have apparently bought out all the remaining inventory.

National inventory data analyzed by CarsDirect brought to broader attention by Motor1 indicates that all new Toyota GR Supra and BMW Z4 units have been sold. (Road & Track found a handful of new Supra and Z4 listings on Autotrader, for what it’s worth, but that info is subject to dealers remembering to update their listings.) Both manufacturers ended production of the sports cars, which were built at the Magna Steyr factory in Austria, back in March.

Despite genuine enthusiast love, neither the GR Supra nor the Z4 sold particularly well. Toyota sold 2953 GR Supras in 2025, while BMW sold 2113 units of the Z4. All told, around 31,228 GR Supra units were sold in the U.S. since 2020. Similarly, BMW sold about 15,282 units of the fifth-generation Z4 in the U.S.

BMW offered a Z4 Final Edition in December 2025 with Individual Frozen Black Metallic paint and a Moonlight Black soft top. Toyota also offered a Final Edition GR Supra in May 2026, featuring larger brakes, adjusted suspension, and matte black paint. 1300 Final Edition GR Supra units made it to the U.S.

Toyota has not officially announced plans for a sixth-generation GR Supra, though company executives said the sports car will likely return. “It would be logical that we would have a next-gen Supra. But when and how is still TBD,” senior vice president of Product Planning and Strategy for Toyota Motor North America Cooper Ericksen said to MotorTrend.

BMW, however, has no current plans to bring a sixth-generation roadster to production. It remains unclear if BMW will bring another roadster to market.

#4648. These Are the Bestselling Electric Pickup Trucks

A total of 232,809 electric pickup trucks have sold since the start of 2024. Ford alone sells nearly that many gas-powered F-series pickups every single quarter.

Electric pickup trucks are still a relatively new idea, but they've now been along long enough to gather some data on how they're selling. We totaled sales numbers from 2024, 2025, and 2026 so far to see which electric pickup trucks have had the biggest impact on the market in the past few years.

For some perspective, electric pickups still make up a tiny portion of the overall truck market in the U.S. Even if you combine the sales of all six models listed here, over a time period of nearly three years, you get 232,809 units sold in total. Ford sold 801,525 units of the F-series pickup in 2025 alone. There are also aren’t any pickup trucks on our list of the bestselling EVs in 2026, a list which contains mostly SUVs.

The sales totals for each model listed here include figures from the full-year 2024, the full-year 2025, and through the third quarter of 2026. In cases where the automaker doesn't release detailed sales figures, we used estimates from Cox Automotive.

If you feel like you see Cybertrucks everywhere you go, that's not just because their distinctive styling makes them stand out on the road. Tesla has sold quite a few pickup trucks in the past few years, which may seem surprising given the Cybertruck's polarizing design and numerous recalls early in its production run. Tesla started selling the Cybertruck in 2024, and that was the strongest year of sales, suggesting that eager early adopters made up much of the early run of 38,965 units sold that year. Sales declined to around 20,000 units in 2025, and through the third quarter of 2026 Tesla has moved an estimated 11,586 units.

Ford was one of the first to enter the electric-truck market, and its strategy hinged on the F-150 Lightning's similarities to the top-selling F-150 pickup. The F-150 Lightning has since been discontinued, ending production in 2025, but it managed to rack up a significant number of sales. Keep in mind that the Lightning went on sale for the 2022 model year, well before many of the other models on this list, so the sales totals here reflect only the latter half of its production run.

General Motors' Hummer EV pickup was also early to the trend, debuting for the 2022 model year like the F-150 Lightning. But it took a completely different approach with its wild styling, mega-horsepower powertrain, and ridiculous off-road capability. GMC added an SUV sibling for 2024, and the caveat to the Hummer's sales numbers are that they include both body styles. We aren't able to break out numbers for just the pickup, because GM doesn't report those figures separately.

Chevy's electric version of the Silverado pickup got off to a slow start, racking up less than 8000 sales in 2024, its first year on the market. Those numbers picked up for 2025 as Chevrolet added lower-cost variants meant for fleets, cresting 11,000 units that year. But it appears demand has softened once again, as Chevy only moved 5327 units through the first three quarters of this year.

Rivian's debut model was the R1T, which was exactly as innovative as you would expect from a startup automaker. With impressive performance, futuristic styling, and new ideas such as a storage tunnel between the cab and the bed, the R1T aimed more at lifestyle buyers than at traditional pickup customers. The R1T went on sale for the 2022 model year, and sales have been on a steady decline since 2024, Rivian's recently launched compact R2 SUV is now outselling the larger R1 lineup, which makes us wonder if there is room for Rivian to add a pickup version of that model that would offer a lower cost of entry.

Riding on the same platform as the Chevrolet Silverado EV, the Sierra EV aims for a middle ground between GM's other electric pickups. It's more upscale than its Chevy sibling, especially in Denali trim, but far more conventional-looking than the other GMC EV truck, the wild Hummer EV. Its sales numbers followed a similar trend as the Chevy, with a slow start in 2024, a rise in 2025, and a drop again in 2026.
